title: Philosophy and worldviews
description: Wonder, fairness, logic and ethics, thinkers from many cultures, and a respectful, neutral look at the world's religious and non-religious worldviews.

nodes.title: Wonder
nodes.description: Ask big questions and enjoy not knowing yet.

nodes.title: Fairness
nodes.description: Think about what is fair and why.

nodes.title: Thinking about thinking
nodes.description: Notice how you know things and when you might be wrong.

nodes.title: Logic
nodes.description: Tell valid arguments from invalid ones and spot fallacies.

competencies.title: Can ask and explore big questions
Can give reasons for an opinion
Can build and test a reasoned argument
Can spot common mistakes in reasoning
Can weigh a moral dilemma from several viewpoints
Can describe several worldviews accurately and respectfully
Can discuss beliefs respectfully with people who differ
Can describe ideas of philosophers from three different cultures

items.subject: wonder
items.title: I wonder...
items.summary: Big questions are fun. There are many possible answers!
steps: 🌙 I wonder... why is the sky dark at night?
🐶 I wonder... do dogs dream?
⭐ I wonder... where does the sky end?
🙋 What do YOU wonder?
🎨 Draw your wonder question.
💭 Ask: what do you think, and why?
items.adultNote: There is no need to give the answer. Say "What do you think?" and "Why?" Wonder is the start of philosophy and science.

items.subject: fairness
items.title: Is it fair?
items.summary: Let's think about sharing and fairness.
steps: 🧸🧸🧸🧸 There are 4 toys and 2 friends.
🤔 Is it fair if one friend gets all 4?
✌️ What if each gets 2?
👶 What if one friend is a baby who can only use 1?
💬 Fair does not always mean the same. Talk about it!

items.subject: festivals
items.title: Festivals of light
items.summary: People all over the world use lights in celebrations.
steps: 🪔 Diwali: Hindus, Sikhs and Jains light lamps and share sweets.
🕎 Hanukkah: Jewish families light candles for eight nights.
🎄 Christmas: many Christians decorate with lights to celebrate the birth of Jesus.
🏮 Lantern Festival: many people in China and elsewhere hang lanterns at the end of the New Year celebrations.
🎨 Draw a paper lantern or lamp.
💬 Do you have a celebration with lights?
items.adultNote: Describe each tradition as "many people who follow this tradition believe..." and never say which is true. Families choose their own approach in settings; this content is for understanding, not for belief. Draw lights rather than using real candles.

items.subject: thinking about thinking
items.title: How do I know?
items.summary: Some things we see, some we are told, some we work out. Let's sort them!
steps: Say three things you know, for example "it is raining" or "the Earth is round".
For each, ask: how do I know? Did I see it, was I told, or did I work it out?
Ask: could I be wrong? How could I check?
Try a trick: look at a straw in a glass of water. Does it look bent? Is it really?
Talk: why is it good to say "I am not sure" sometimes?

items.subject: wonder
items.title: Is it still the same tower?
items.summary: An ancient puzzle: if you change every part of something, is it still the same thing?
steps: Build a tower from 6 blocks, cups or boxes.
Swap one block for a new one. Is it the same tower?
Keep swapping until every block is new. Same tower now?
What if you rebuild a tower with all the old blocks? Which one is the "real" one?
Greek thinkers told this puzzle about a ship called the Ship of Theseus.
Think: you are always growing new cells. Are you the same you as when you were a baby?

items.subject: worldviews
items.title: People believe different things
items.summary: Around the world, people have different ideas about big questions like how the world began and how to live well.
steps: Some people follow a religion, such as Buddhism, Christianity, Hinduism, Islam, Judaism or Sikhism.
Some people are not religious. Some call themselves humanists, atheists or agnostics.
Many people mix traditions, or follow local and Indigenous traditions.
People in the same family can believe different things.
We can learn about beliefs with curiosity and respect, even if we believe something different.
Talk with your family: what matters most to us?

check.question: If a friend believes something different from you, it is kind to...
check.explain: Yes. Respect lets everyone learn from each other.

items.adultNote: Describe each tradition as "many people who follow this tradition believe..." and never say which is true. Families choose their own approach in settings; this content is for understanding, not for belief.

items.subject: reasons
items.title: Because...
items.summary: An opinion is stronger when you give a good reason.
steps: Say an opinion: "Cats make better pets than dogs."
Add "because" and a reason.
Is it a strong reason or a weak one? "Because I said so" is weak!
Strong reasons can be checked, are relevant, and would make sense to other people.
Play: one person gives an opinion, the other must give the best reason for the opposite view.
Change your mind if you hear a better reason - that is clever, not weak.

check.question: Which is the stronger reason for "We should walk to the park"?
options: "Because it is close and the weather is nice."
check.explain: Yes. It gives facts others can check.

items.subject: beliefs and practices
items.title: A tour of world worldviews
items.summary: Learn what followers of some major worldviews believe and practise, in their own terms.
steps: Buddhism: many Buddhists follow the teachings of the Buddha about ending suffering, including kindness and meditation.
Christianity: Christians believe in one God and follow the teachings of Jesus, whom they believe is the Son of God.
Hinduism: a family of traditions; many Hindus believe in a supreme reality (Brahman) shown in many forms, and in dharma (right living) and rebirth.
Islam: Muslims believe in one God (Allah) and follow the Qur'an and the example of the Prophet Muhammad.
Judaism: Jews believe in one God who made a covenant with the Jewish people, and follow the Torah.
Sikhism: Sikhs believe in one God and follow the teachings of the Gurus, written in the Guru Granth Sahib.
Non-religious worldviews: humanists, for example, look to reason, evidence and shared human values to decide how to live.
Make a chart: name, main beliefs, holy texts or key ideas, places to gather, one festival.

check.question: Which sentence is the respectful way to describe a belief?
check.explain: Yes. We describe what people believe without judging which is right.

items.adultNote: Describe each tradition as "many people who follow this tradition believe..." and never say which is true. Families choose their own approach in settings; this content is for understanding, not for belief. There are many other traditions (for example Jainism, Bahá'í, Shinto, Daoism, Zoroastrianism and Indigenous traditions) worth exploring too.

items.subject: philosophers
items.title: Thinkers from around the world
items.summary: People in every part of the world have asked big questions. Meet some of them.
steps: Confucius (China, about 2,500 years ago) taught about kindness, respect and how to be a good person in a family and a state.
Siddhartha Gautama, the Buddha (South Asia, about 2,500 years ago), taught about the causes of suffering and how to end it.
Socrates (ancient Athens) asked people questions to test what they really knew.
Hypatia (Alexandria, Egypt, about 1,600 years ago) taught mathematics, astronomy and philosophy.
Ibn Rushd (Córdoba, in what is now Spain, about 850 years ago) wrote about reason, faith and the ideas of Aristotle.
Zera Yacob (Ethiopia, about 400 years ago) wrote about using reason to search for truth.
Pick one thinker. Write one question they might ask you today.

items.subject: logic
items.title: If... then... logic
items.summary: Logic helps us see whether a conclusion really follows from its reasons.
steps: An argument has premises (reasons) and a conclusion.
Valid: "All cats are mammals. Tom is a cat. So Tom is a mammal."
An argument can be valid but have a false premise: "All birds can fly. Penguins are birds. So penguins can fly." The logic works, but the first premise is false.
Watch out for this trap: "If it rains, the ground is wet. The ground is wet. So it rained." Not valid - a hose could have done it!
Write three arguments of your own: one valid and true, one valid with a false premise, one invalid.
Swap with someone and test each other.

check.question: "If it rains, the ground is wet. The ground is wet, so it rained." This is...
check.explain: Invalid. Something else could have made the ground wet.

items.subject: logic
items.title: Fallacy hunt
items.summary: Fallacies are tricks or mistakes in reasoning. Learn five and hunt for them.
steps: Attacking the person: "Don't listen to her, she's young." (ignores the argument)
Straw man: twisting someone's view into a weaker one, then knocking it down.
Bandwagon: "Everyone is buying it, so it must be good."
False choice: "Either you agree with me or you don't care at all."
Slippery slope: "If we allow this, disaster will surely follow" (without evidence for each step).
Look at adverts, posters or arguments in conversations. Find one example of each.
Rewrite one so it uses a fair reason instead.
items.adultNote: Use examples from a range of sources and views so the focus is reasoning, not taking sides.

items.subject: ethics
items.title: Tricky choices
items.summary: Philosophers have different ways of deciding what is right. Try them on a tricky choice.
steps: Dilemma: you promised to meet a friend, but on the way you see a neighbour who needs help carrying shopping. What do you do?
Consequences: which choice leads to the best results for everyone?
Duties and rules: what promises or duties do you have?
Virtues: what would a kind, honest, brave person do?
Care: who depends on you, and how will they feel?
Many religious and non-religious traditions also offer guidance, such as versions of "treat others as you would like to be treated".
Write your choice and the reasons from two different approaches.

check.question: Asking "what would a kind and honest person do?" is which approach?
check.explain: Yes. Virtue ethics asks what a person of good character would do.

items.subject: beliefs and practices
items.title: Comparing practices
items.summary: Compare how different traditions mark life events, gather and reflect.
steps: Pick three worldviews, including at least one non-religious one.
Research: how do people mark a birth, coming of age, marriage or death?
Research: where do people gather, and what do they do there?
Research: are there food customs, fasting or special clothes?
Make a comparison table. Look for similarities as well as differences.
Note where people within one tradition do things differently from each other.
Use sources written by members of each tradition, plus a neutral encyclopedia.
items.adultNote: Describe each tradition as "many people who follow this tradition believe..." and never say which is true. Families choose their own approach in settings; this content is for understanding, not for belief.

items.subject: argument
items.title: Write a philosophical argument
items.summary: Write a short essay that answers a big question with a careful argument, then answer the best objection.
steps: Choose a question, such as "Is it ever right to break a promise?" or "Can machines think?"
Write your answer in one sentence (your thesis).
List your premises. Check each one: is it true? Does the conclusion follow?
Find the strongest objection someone could make.
Write a reply to the objection - or change your view if it wins!
Write it up in 600-1000 words.
Read it to someone and ask them to argue back.

better.description: Read what two philosophers said about your question and include them.

advanced.description: Type, edit and share the essay; record a discussion about it.

substitutions.use: Free public-domain texts or a free online encyclopedia of philosophy
Write the objection and reply as a dialogue between two characters

items.subject: dialogue
items.title: Listening across worldviews
items.summary: Learn about someone's beliefs or values by asking good questions and listening respectfully.
steps: With an adult, choose someone known to your family to talk to, or a published interview or autobiography.
Prepare open questions: "What matters most to you?" "What do you celebrate and why?"
Listen to understand, not to argue. Repeat back what you heard.
Do not ask people to justify or defend their beliefs unless they want to.
Write a short summary they would agree is fair.
Reflect: what did you learn, and what do you share with them?
items.adultNote: Describe each tradition as "many people who follow this tradition believe..." and never say which is true. Families choose their own approach in settings; this content is for understanding, not for belief. Arrange and supervise any interview; never with strangers online.

items.subject: ethics
items.title: Big ethical questions today
items.summary: Use ethics to think about real modern questions where thoughtful people disagree.
steps: Choose one: how should we treat animals? Who is responsible when AI makes a mistake? What do we owe future generations?
List the people (and animals) affected.
Apply two approaches: consequences and duties/rights.
Find two thoughtful people or organisations who disagree, and summarise each view fairly.
Say where you stand and what evidence could change your mind.

items.subject: thinking about thinking
items.title: How do we know what we know?
items.summary: Epistemology is the study of knowledge. When should we believe something?
steps: Sources of knowledge: our senses, reasoning, memory and testimony (what others tell us).
Each can mislead: senses are tricked by illusions, memories change, people make mistakes.
Science tests ideas with evidence and lets other people check the results.
Good thinkers match how strongly they believe to how strong the evidence is.
Note that some questions (like what makes life meaningful) are explored through philosophy and worldviews as well as science.
Pick a belief you hold. Rate your confidence 1-10 and list the evidence.

check.question: Good thinkers believe something...
options: as strongly as the evidence supports
as strongly as they want to
check.explain: Yes. Match your confidence to the evidence.

items.subject: kindness
items.title: Is it kind?
items.summary: Let us think: what makes something kind? Say why!
steps: 🧸 Sharing a toy. Kind? 👍 or 👎
😢 A friend falls down. You help them up. Kind?
🙊 Saying a mean word. Kind?
🤔 Say why: "It is kind because..."
💛 Think of one kind thing you can do today.

check.question: A friend is sad. What is kind?

items.adultNote: Ask "why?" and "how would they feel?" rather than giving the answer. Notice and name real kind acts during the day.

items.subject: celebrations
items.title: How families celebrate
items.summary: Families celebrate special days in different ways. How does yours?
steps: 🎂 Some families have a cake and sing songs.
🍲 Some families cook a special meal together.
🏮 Some families light lamps or wear new clothes.
👵 Some families visit grandparents or friends.
🖍️ Draw your family's special day. What do you like best?

check.question: Do all families celebrate in the same way?
check.explain: Yes! Families celebrate in many different ways.

check.question: Your friend celebrates differently. You can...
check.explain: Yes! Asking kindly helps us learn about each other.

items.adultNote: Keep it descriptive and neutral: "some families...". Include birthdays and family days, and families who do not mark religious festivals. No family way is better than another.

items.subject: wonder
items.title: What makes a friend?
items.summary: A big question with no single right answer. Think, give reasons and listen to others.
steps: Sit with a grown-up or friends. The big question is: what makes someone a friend?
Each person says one idea and starts with "I think... because...".
Try harder questions: Can a pet be a friend? Can you be friends with someone far away?
Listen. Did someone say something that made you change your mind?
Draw a picture of what friendship means to you.

check.question: Two people have different answers to a big question. What is a good thing to do?
check.explain: With big questions, listening to reasons helps everyone think more.

items.adultNote: There is no correct answer. Ask "why do you think that?" and "can you give an example?" rather than correcting ideas.
